name: Old Kingdom Egypt

P1.justification: Centralized bureaucracy with vizier, provincial nomarchs, and royal court; one of the earliest documented complex administrative states, but nomarch autonomy grew in Dynasties 5-6.
quantitative_anchors: Seshat: polity territory ~1M km2 at peak; hierarchical levels = 4-5 (Turchin et al. 2018)

P2.justification: Pyramid construction demonstrates advanced surveying, engineering, and logistical coordination; medical papyri and astronomical observation present but no systematic diffusion mechanism.
quantitative_anchors: Great Pyramid: 2.3M blocks, ~20yr construction; earliest known surgical text (Edwin Smith Papyrus) dates to OK copies

P3.justification: Scribal schools for elite, life expectancy ~30-35 years typical of Bronze Age agricultural societies; population sufficient for large-scale labor mobilization.
quantitative_anchors: Butzer estimates population 1.5-2M; literacy confined to <1% scribal class

P4.justification: Redistributive palace economy with organized agriculture, quarrying, and Nile-based trade; limited long-distance commerce compared to later periods.
quantitative_anchors: Maddison Project: Egypt c.1 CE ~$700 GK$; OK necessarily lower, proxy ~$400-500 range

P5.justification: Stable for ~500 years (Dynasties 3-5), but 4.2 kiloyear climate event and rising nomarch autonomy eroded central control in Dynasty 6.
quantitative_anchors: 4.2 kyr event: Nile flood failures documented; First Intermediate Period begins c.2181 BCE

name: Achaemenid Persia

P1.justification: Satrapal system governing 20-30 provinces with standardized tribute, Royal Road communications, codified law (Darius's Ordinance of Good Regulations), and imperial inspectors ('King's Eyes') — the most sophisticated pre-modern administrative apparatus.
quantitative_anchors: Seshat: hierarchical levels = 6; 20-31 satrapies; Royal Road ~2,700 km with relay stations

P2.justification: Standardized coinage (daric), cuneiform administrative records, advanced irrigation (qanat systems), and deliberate knowledge synthesis across subject peoples.
quantitative_anchors: Persepolis Fortification Archive: ~30,000 tablets documenting bureaucratic sophistication

P3.justification: Multi-ethnic empire with variable human development across satrapies; Babylonian and Egyptian regions had higher literacy/health than peripheral areas.
quantitative_anchors: Aperghis estimates total population ~35M; Briant notes ~17M in core Iranian/Mesopotamian provinces

P4.justification: Standardized weights/measures, Royal Road enabling long-distance trade, monetized economy in western satrapies, and tribute-based revenue system.
quantitative_anchors: Herodotus records annual tribute ~14,560 Euboic talents; daric gold standard weight 8.4g

P5.justification: Empire endured ~220 years through multiple succession crises and Greek Wars; collapse was exogenous (Alexander's conquest), not structural failure.
quantitative_anchors: Empire span 550-330 BCE; survived revolts in Egypt (404-343 BCE) and Babylon before Macedonian conquest

bibliography: Aperghis, G.G. (2004). The Seleukid Royal Economy. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Briant, P. (2002). From Cyrus to Alexander: A History of the Persian Empire. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.
Root, M.C. (1979). The King and Kingship in Achaemenid Art. Leiden: Brill.
Wiesehöfer, J. (2001). Ancient Persia: From 550 BC to 650 AD. London: I.B. Tauris.
note: ORDINAL (1-5, relative to contemporaries). Grounded in Briant's comprehensive reconstruction and Persepolis Fortification Archive evidence. Peak scores reflect pre-Alexandrian zenith; pre_stress = peak because collapse was exogenous conquest, not internal deterioration. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Sasanian Persia

P1.justification: At peak (Khosrow I): centralized tax reform, salaried army replacing feudal levies, four-quarter administrative division. Pre-stress (post-Khosrow II): exhaustion from 26-year Byzantine war, noble factionalism, rapid succession of rulers.
quantitative_anchors: Pourshariati documents 12 rulers in final 14 years (628-642); Khosrow I's tax reform yielded ~420M dirhams annually

P2.justification: Academy of Gundishapur synthesized Greek, Indian, and Persian knowledge; advanced irrigation, metallurgy, and textile production.
quantitative_anchors: Gundishapur active c.3rd-7th century; Sasanian silver plate production among finest metalwork of late antiquity

P3.justification: Rigid caste system (priests, warriors, scribes, commoners) limited social mobility; Zoroastrian priestly literacy but narrow diffusion.
quantitative_anchors: Morony estimates Iraq population alone ~8-9M pre-conquest; total empire ~20-25M

P4.justification: Controlled east-west Silk Road transit; monetized economy with silver drachm standard; state-managed irrigation in Mesopotamia.
quantitative_anchors: Silk Road transit taxes significant revenue source; Sasanian drachm widely circulated from Central Asia to Ethiopia

P5.justification: Even at peak, dynastic succession was contested and noble houses held military power. Pre-stress: exhausted by 602-628 Byzantine war, plague, and noble confederacy fragmentation — structurally unable to resist Arab conquest.
quantitative_anchors: 602-628 war cost estimated at half the empire's revenue; Battle of al-Qadisiyyah (636) decided by ~30,000 Arab troops against a fractured Sasanian force

bibliography: Daryaee, T. (2009). Sasanian Persia: The Rise and Fall of an Empire. London: I.B. Tauris.
Morony, M. (1984). Iraq After the Muslim Conquest. Princeton: Princeton University Press.

Simpson, St J. (2017). Sasanian Elites and Their Legacy. BAR International Series.
note: ORDINAL (1-5, relative to contemporaries). Grounded in Pourshariati's confederacy thesis and Daryaee's institutional analysis. Large gap between peak and pre-stress reflects documented institutional collapse. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Mauryan Empire

P1.justification: Arthashastra describes a sophisticated bureaucratic apparatus with espionage networks, provincial governors, and treasury management. But institutional quality was ruler-dependent — collapsed rapidly after Ashoka.
quantitative_anchors: Arthashastra describes 18 tirthas (ministerial offices); Ashoka's 33 rock/pillar edicts across subcontinent show administrative reach

P2.justification: Polished stone pillar technology, Mauryan punch-marked coinage, and urban planning at Pataliputra; knowledge production present but not systematically diffused beyond court.
quantitative_anchors: Pataliputra estimated at ~150,000-300,000 population (Megasthenes via Strabo); advanced metallurgy in pillar construction

P3.justification: Ashoka's edicts indicate concern for public welfare (hospitals, veterinary clinics, road shade trees), but literacy remained elite and life expectancy was standard for ancient agrarian empires.
quantitative_anchors: Maddison: Indian subcontinent GDP/cap ~$450 GK$ c.1 CE, Mauryan era likely similar; total population ~30M (Maddison estimate)

P4.justification: Extensive trade routes (Royal Highway), monetized economy, and agricultural surplus. Pre-stress P4 higher than P1 reflects the classic P4>P1 gap: commercial networks outlasted institutional control.
quantitative_anchors: Royal Highway: Pataliputra to Taxila ~1,600 km; Kautilya's Arthashastra details state monopolies on mines, forests, salt

P5.justification: Under Chandragupta and Ashoka, stability maintained through standing army and intelligence apparatus. Post-Ashoka succession weakness led to rapid fragmentation — last Maurya assassinated by general Pushyamitra.
quantitative_anchors: Pliny/Megasthenes: standing army of 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry (likely exaggerated but indicates scale); dynasty collapsed ~50 years after Ashoka's death

bibliography: Allchin, B. & Allchin, R. (1982). The Rise of Civilization in India and Pakistan. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Thapar, R. (2012). Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas. 3rd ed. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
note: ORDINAL (1-5, relative to contemporaries). Grounded in Thapar's standard work and the Arthashastra (Olivelle translation). The P4>P1 gap at pre-stress is the central diagnostic finding. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Gupta Empire

P1.justification: Looser feudal-style governance compared to Maurya; provincial autonomy always significant. Peak P1 only 3 because institutional control was indirect — land grants (agrahara) devolved authority structurally.
quantitative_anchors: Fa-Xian (c.405 CE) describes light-touch governance; copper-plate land grants document devolution

P2.justification: Golden age of Indian science: Aryabhata (astronomy/mathematics, c.499 CE), Varahamihira, Nalanda university, Ajanta cave art, Sanskrit literary florescence (Kalidasa).
quantitative_anchors: Aryabhata calculated Earth's circumference to within 0.2%; Nalanda housed ~10,000 students (Xuanzang, 7th c.)

P3.justification: Elite education at Nalanda and other centers; caste system constrained broad human development; life expectancy typical of agrarian empires.
quantitative_anchors: Maddison: Indian subcontinent GDP/cap ~$450 GK$ c.500 CE; population ~75M subcontinent

P4.justification: Extensive Indian Ocean and overland trade; Gupta gold coinage among finest in ancient world; spice, textile, and gemstone exports to Rome and Southeast Asia.
quantitative_anchors: Gupta gold dinar weight ~8g, high purity; maritime trade to SE Asia established Indianized kingdoms

P5.justification: Stable under Chandragupta II (r.380-415), but Huna/Hephthalite invasions from c.450 combined with feudatory rebellion to fragment the empire by c.550.
quantitative_anchors: Skandagupta repelled first Huna invasion c.455; by c.550 Gupta territory reduced to Magadha heartland

bibliography: Bakker, H. (1997). The Vakatakas: An Essay in Hindu Iconology. Groningen: Egbert Forsten.

note: ORDINAL (1-5, relative to contemporaries). Grounded in Basham/Kulke standard histories and Maddison GDP estimates. 'Golden age' tag reflects P2=4 (high innovation) alongside moderate P1 (weak institutions) — the P4>P1 gap is diagnostic. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Vijayanagara

P1.justification: Nayaka provincial system with significant local autonomy; central authority depended on military control and tributary relationships rather than bureaucratic depth.
quantitative_anchors: Abdur Razzaq (1443) and Paes (c.1520) describe elaborate court but devolved provincial governance; ~200 nayaka chiefs

P2.justification: Sophisticated temple architecture, irrigation engineering, and textile production; knowledge economy present but not systematically advancing beyond regional norms.
quantitative_anchors: Hampi ruins cover 26 km2; Virupaksha temple complex among largest in South India

P3.justification: Caste hierarchy limited broad human development; temple schools provided limited education; life expectancy typical of medieval South Asian agrarian states.
quantitative_anchors: Maddison: Indian subcontinent GDP/cap ~$550 GK$ c.1500; Hampi population estimated 250,000-500,000 at peak

P4.justification: Major spice and textile exporter; controlled key Indian Ocean trade routes; Portuguese accounts describe thriving commerce at Hampi's bazaars.
quantitative_anchors: Paes describes Hampi bazaars 'as large as those of Lisbon'; diamond trade at Golconda; horse imports from Arabia

P5.justification: Survived 200+ years in hostile strategic environment (Bahmani/Deccan sultanates), but Battle of Talikota (1565) destroyed the capital and fragmented the empire into successor nayaka states.
quantitative_anchors: Battle of Talikota 1565: combined sultanate forces ~100,000; Hampi sacked and abandoned within months

bibliography: Eaton, R. (2005). A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Karashima, N. (2014). A Concise History of South India. New Delhi: Oxford University Press.

note: ORDINAL (1-5, relative to contemporaries). Grounded in Stein's standard monograph and Portuguese traveler accounts (Paes, Nuniz). P4>P1 gap diagnostic — commercial strength exceeded institutional depth. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Tang Dynasty

P1.justification: Mature civil-service examination system, codified Tang Code (624 CE), Six Ministries, provincial governor system. Peak represents pre-An Lushan era; pre_stress reflects jiedushi (military governor) autonomy after 755.
quantitative_anchors: Tang Code: 502 articles in 30 chapters; exam system selected ~30 jinshi/year; Seshat hierarchical levels = 6

P2.justification: Woodblock printing (earliest dated: 868 CE Diamond Sutra), porcelain mass production, gunpowder formulation, advanced agricultural techniques (Jiangnan rice cultivation).
quantitative_anchors: 868 CE Diamond Sutra is earliest dated printed book; porcelain exports reached Abbasid Baghdad and East Africa

P3.justification: Examination system created meritocratic pathway; urban literacy higher than contemporaries; cosmopolitan culture in Chang'an drew scholars from across Eurasia.
quantitative_anchors: Maddison: China GDP/cap ~$480 GK$ at Tang peak; Bielenstein estimates population 50-60M, reaching 80M by 750s; Chang'an population ~1M

P4.justification: Silk Road apex; Grand Canal completed linking north-south; monetized economy with kaiyuan tongbao coinage. Post-An Lushan trade disruption and fiscal fragmentation reduced P4.
quantitative_anchors: Grand Canal: ~1,800 km linking Hangzhou to Beijing; annual salt revenue alone ~millions of strings of cash

P5.justification: Stable for 130 years before An Lushan rebellion (755) killed ~36M (Bielenstein census analysis) and permanently shifted power to military governors. Final collapse through Huang Chao rebellion (874-884).
quantitative_anchors: An Lushan: census drops from 52.9M (754) to 16.9M (764) — partly displacement, partly mortality; Five Dynasties fragmentation followed by 907

bibliography: Hansen, V. (2000). The Open Empire: A History of China to 1600. New York: W.W. Norton.
Lewis, M.E. (2009). China's Cosmopolitan Empire: The Tang Dynasty. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.

note: ORDINAL (1-5, relative to contemporaries). Grounded in Cambridge History of China and Maddison GDP estimates. Tang scores among highest in ancient corpus; An Lushan rebellion is the key structural break. Census data provides unusually strong quantitative anchor. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Song Dynasty

P1.justification: Most developed pre-modern civil bureaucracy: expanded examination system selecting ~200+ jinshi/year by Southern Song, professionalized fiscal administration, codified commercial law.
quantitative_anchors: Exam candidates: ~400,000 per cycle by Southern Song; civil service ~20,000 officials governing ~100M people

P2.justification: Movable type printing (Bi Sheng c.1040), magnetic compass for navigation, gunpowder weapons, hydraulic engineering, and the world's first paper currency (jiaozi). Strongest pre-modern innovation case.
quantitative_anchors: Elvin's 'medieval economic revolution': iron production ~125,000 tons/year by 1078 (not exceeded in Europe until 18th c.)

P3.justification: Highest pre-modern literacy rates outside classical Athens; widespread printing made books affordable; urban culture and commercial schools.
quantitative_anchors: Maddison: China GDP/cap >$600 GK$ at Song peak — highest in world; population ~100-120M; urbanization rate ~10-12% (Rozman)

P4.justification: World's most commercialized pre-modern economy: paper currency, maritime trade dominance, proto-industrial production, and tax revenue exceeding all contemporaries.
quantitative_anchors: Annual government revenue ~60M strings of cash (Northern Song); maritime customs revenue from Guangzhou, Quanzhou; Shiba documents 'commercial revolution'

P5.justification: Northern Song fell to Jurchen Jin (1127) — survived as Southern Song for another 152 years. Final collapse to Mongols (1279) was exogenous military conquest, not internal fragmentation.
quantitative_anchors: Southern Song defended against Mongols for 45 years (1234-1279); naval battle of Yamen (1279) ended dynasty

Highest-scoring ancient case; collapse was purely exogenous (Mongol conquest). Maddison GDP data and iron production figures provide strong quantitative anchors. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Tokugawa Japan

P1.justification: Bakuhan system: centralized shogunal authority over ~260 semi-autonomous domains (han); sankin-kotai (alternate attendance) as institutional control mechanism; Confucian bureaucratic norms.
quantitative_anchors: 260+ han domains; sankin-kotai required biennial residence in Edo; shogunal direct domain ~15% of total rice yield

P2.justification: Rangaku (Dutch learning) provided narrow Western science channel; sophisticated craft production (swords, ceramics, textiles) but sakoku policy limited systematic innovation diffusion.
quantitative_anchors: Rangaku: ~500 Dutch books imported/translated by late Tokugawa; Dejima trade post sole Western contact

P3.justification: Exceptionally high literacy for pre-modern state: terakoya (temple schools) and domain schools produced ~40% male literacy by 1850s. Life expectancy comparable to early modern Europe.
quantitative_anchors: Dore: male literacy ~40-45% by 1860s, female ~15%; ~15,000 terakoya by Bakumatsu period; Maddison GDP/cap ~$570 GK$ c.1700, ~$669 by 1820

P4.justification: Sophisticated domestic economy with rice-based exchange system, proto-industrial putting-out system (Osaka cotton), and castle-town commerce. Sakoku limited external trade but internal markets were highly developed.
quantitative_anchors: Maddison: Japan GDP/cap ~$570 GK$ c.1700, rising to ~$669 by 1820; Edo population ~1M by 1720 (largest city in world)

P5.justification: 250 years of internal peace (Pax Tokugawa, 1615-1868) — one of the longest stable periods for any pre-modern polity. Pre-stress decline reflects Perry shock (1853) and mounting domain debts.
quantitative_anchors: 1615-1868: 253 years without major internal conflict; Meiji Restoration (1868) was managed transition, not state collapse

Uniquely high P5 (250yr peace); managed transition outcome distinguishes it from rupture cases. Maddison GDP and Dore literacy rates are strong quantitative anchors. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Joseon Korea

P1.justification: Neo-Confucian bureaucratic state with competitive civil service examinations (gwageo), Six Ministries, censorate (Saheonbu), and codified law (Gyeongguk daejeon, 1485). Institutional depth sustained dynasty for 500+ years.
quantitative_anchors: Gwageo exams selected ~33 munkwa (civil) + 28 mugwa (military) per triennial cycle; Gyeongguk daejeon codified in 6 volumes

P2.justification: Hangul alphabet creation (1443) is major innovation; movable metal type (jikji, 1377 predates Gutenberg); rain gauge (cheugugi, 1441). But neo-Confucian orthodoxy limited sustained technological change.
quantitative_anchors: Jikji (1377): earliest surviving movable metal type printed book; Hangul: 28-letter phonemic alphabet designed for mass literacy

P3.justification: Yangban elite literacy very high; commoner education limited by rigid social hierarchy (yangban/jungin/sangmin/cheonmin). Hangul improved potential literacy but social barriers persisted.
quantitative_anchors: Maddison: Korea GDP/cap ~$600 GK$ c.1820; population ~10-14M by late Joseon

P4.justification: Agrarian economy with limited commercial development compared to Tokugawa Japan; tributary trade with Ming/Qing; internal markets constrained by Confucian anti-commerce ideology.
quantitative_anchors: Maddison: Korea GDP/cap ~$600 GK$ c.1820, roughly comparable to Japan but with less commercial development

P5.justification: Survived Imjin War (1592-98) Japanese invasion and Manchu invasions (1627, 1636) — remarkable institutional resilience. Reconstruction capacity after Imjin War is the key diagnostic observation.
quantitative_anchors: Imjin War: estimated 1-2M Korean deaths; post-war reconstruction restored administrative capacity within ~50 years; dynasty endured 518 years total (1392-1910)

name: Khmer / Angkor

P1.justification: Devaraja (god-king) system with provincial administration through appointed governors; temple-based bureaucracy with Sanskrit/Khmer inscription records. Sophisticated but personalized around royal court.
quantitative_anchors: ~1,000+ inscriptions document administrative structure; Zhou Daguan (1296) provides detailed court/governance account

P2.justification: Baray (reservoir) water management system among most sophisticated pre-modern hydraulic engineering; Angkor Wat architectural achievement, but limited evidence of systematic knowledge diffusion.
quantitative_anchors: West Baray: 8km x 2.3km, ~56M m3 capacity; Angkor Wat: largest religious monument, 162.6 hectares

P3.justification: Large urban population supported by rice surplus agriculture; temple education for elites; life expectancy typical of tropical agrarian states.
quantitative_anchors: Evans et al. LiDAR: Greater Angkor urban complex ~1,000 km2; population estimates revised upward to 750,000-1,000,000

P4.justification: Regional trade hub connecting China and India via maritime Southeast Asian routes; Tonle Sap fishery and rice surplus supported large non-agricultural population. Trade decline preceded political collapse.
quantitative_anchors: Zhou Daguan (1296) describes Chinese merchants, gold/silver trade, and specialized craft production at Angkor

P5.justification: Angkorian state lasted 600+ years but was periodically contested. Final decline involved Thai (Ayutthaya) military pressure, water management failure, and capital relocation — a migrate/transform outcome, not a rupture.
quantitative_anchors: Buckley et al.: tree-ring data shows severe droughts c.1345-1375 and 1401-1425, coinciding with state contraction; Angkor abandoned as capital by c.1431

name: Srivijaya

P1.justification: Maritime mandala polity with minimal territorial bureaucracy; power exercised through trade control and ritual authority rather than institutional administration. The archetype of extreme P4>P1 gap.
quantitative_anchors: Only ~12 Old Malay inscriptions survive (7th c.); Yijing (671 CE) describes Palembang as a learning center but not a bureaucratic capital

P2.justification: Buddhist learning center attracting monks from China and India; maritime navigation and shipbuilding knowledge; but limited evidence of systematic technological innovation.
quantitative_anchors: Yijing: ~1,000 Buddhist monks at Palembang c.671; Nalanda-level Buddhist scholarship described

P3.justification: Buddhist monastic education for elites; general population primarily engaged in maritime commerce and agriculture; limited data on broader human development indicators.
quantitative_anchors: Population estimates highly uncertain; Palembang/coastal populations perhaps 20,000-50,000 in core

P4.justification: Controlled Strait of Malacca chokepoint — the most important pre-modern maritime trade route between Indian Ocean and South China Sea. Extreme trade dominance relative to institutional capacity.
quantitative_anchors: Arab/Chinese sources describe Srivijaya as dominant entrepôt for 7th-11th c. maritime trade; Chola raid (1025) targeted trade infrastructure specifically

P5.justification: Maintained Strait hegemony for ~400 years despite minimal institutional depth — impressive resilience for a thalassocracy. Chola naval raids (1025) disrupted but didn't immediately destroy; final fragmentation was gradual.
quantitative_anchors: Rajendra Chola I raid (1025): captured 14 Srivijayan ports; polity fragmented into competing port-states by 13th century

note: ORDINAL (1-5, relative to contemporaries). Grounded in Manguin's archaeological synthesis and Chinese/Arab textual sources. P4=5 vs P1=2 is the most extreme pillar gap in the ancient corpus — the thalassocracy archetype. MOD data quality reflects limited epigraphy. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Majapahit

P1.justification: Mandala polity: inner core directly administered, outer ring of semi-autonomous tributaries. Nagarakretagama (1365) describes extensive claims but real administrative control was limited beyond Java. Declined after Hayam Wuruk's death (1389).
quantitative_anchors: Nagarakretagama lists ~98 tributaries but most were nominal; Ming Shi records diplomatic missions from Majapahit

P2.justification: Sophisticated literary culture (Nagarakretagama, Sutasoma), temple architecture (Trowulan complex), and metallurgy; knowledge production comparable to regional contemporaries.
quantitative_anchors: Trowulan site: ~100 km2 urban complex; Chinese ceramics and local terracotta production documented archaeologically

P3.justification: Court literary culture and Buddhist-Hindu religious education; general population primarily agrarian with limited access to formal education.
quantitative_anchors: Trowulan population estimated at 200,000-500,000; Java total population perhaps 4-5M (Reid estimates)

P4.justification: Major spice trade hub controlling eastern Indonesian spice islands (clove, nutmeg, pepper); Chinese, Indian, and Arab merchants documented at Javanese ports.
quantitative_anchors: Spice trade: cloves and nutmeg exclusively from eastern Indonesia; Ma Huan (1433) describes Javanese commerce

P5.justification: Stable under Hayam Wuruk (r.1350-1389) with Gajah Mada as chief minister. Succession crisis of Paregreg civil war (1405-06) fatally weakened central authority; Islamic coastal states progressively detached.
quantitative_anchors: Paregreg war (1405-06): split between eastern and western court factions; Demak (Islamic) successor established by 1478

name: Mali Empire

P1.justification: Provincial administration through farba (governors) and local chiefs; Mansa held authority through lineage legitimacy and military control. Administrative capacity peaked under Mansa Musa (r.1312-1337) but was ruler-dependent.
quantitative_anchors: Ibn Battuta (1352) describes functioning court, judges (qadi), and provincial governors; ~14 provinces reported in Arabic sources

P2.justification: Timbuktu and Djenné as Islamic learning centers; Sankore mosque/university attracted scholars from across Muslim world. Agricultural and metallurgical knowledge present but not systematically documented.
quantitative_anchors: Sankore: estimated 25,000 students at peak (likely exaggerated but indicates scale); manuscript traditions survive in Timbuktu libraries

P3.justification: Islamic education available in urban centers (Timbuktu, Djenné, Niani); rural majority had limited formal education. Life expectancy typical of sub-Saharan agrarian societies.
quantitative_anchors: McEvedy & Jones: West African savanna population ~15-20M in region; urban populations modest (Timbuktu ~50,000-100,000 at peak)

P4.justification: Controlled trans-Saharan gold trade — at peak, Mali supplied roughly half of Old World gold. Mansa Musa's 1324 hajj reportedly depressed Cairo gold prices for a decade. Extreme P4>P1 gap.
quantitative_anchors: Mansa Musa hajj (1324): reportedly carried 12,000+ kg of gold; al-Umari reports Cairo gold price depression lasting years; Bambuk/Buré goldfields dominant global source

P5.justification: Stable for ~150 years under strong mansas. Decline driven by succession disputes and Songhai/Mossi/Tuareg pressure from multiple directions simultaneously.
quantitative_anchors: Empire span ~1235-1600; Songhai under Sunni Ali captured Timbuktu 1468; by c.1500 Mali reduced to Manding heartland

bibliography: Austen, R. (2010). Trans-Saharan Africa in World History. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
Insoll, T. (2003). The Archaeology of Islam in Sub-Saharan Africa. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

note: ORDINAL (1-5, relative to contemporaries). Grounded in Levtzion's standard history and Arabic primary sources (Ibn Battuta, al-Umari). P4=5 reflects documented gold trade dominance; MOD data quality due to reliance on external (Arabic) sources for internal history. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Great Zimbabwe

P1.justification: Centralized authority evidenced by monumental stone architecture (Great Enclosure) and control of cattle wealth and trade goods. No writing system — governance reconstructed from archaeology and oral tradition.
quantitative_anchors: Great Enclosure: 11m high walls, 250m circumference, largest pre-colonial stone structure in sub-Saharan Africa; ~182 stone enclosures at site

P2.justification: Sophisticated dry-stone construction without mortar; iron and copper smelting; gold working. But no writing system and limited evidence of systematic knowledge production beyond craft specialization.
quantitative_anchors: Iron smelting furnaces documented archaeologically; gold ornaments and crucibles recovered from Hill Complex

P3.justification: No writing system limits evidence; population supported by cattle pastoralism and agriculture. Lower score reflects absence of documented formal education or health infrastructure.
quantitative_anchors: Peak urban population estimated ~18,000 (Pikirayi); cattle kraal capacity suggests substantial herds

P4.justification: Indian Ocean trade link via Sofala coast: exported gold, ivory, and iron; imported Chinese ceramics, glass beads, and cloth. Trade wealth disproportionate to institutional capacity.
quantitative_anchors: Chinese celadon and Middle Eastern glass beads recovered archaeologically; gold exports to Kilwa/Sofala documented by al-Masudi and later Portuguese

P5.justification: Polity endured ~300 years (c.1100-1450); decline linked to environmental degradation (deforestation, soil exhaustion) and trade route shifts. Successor states Mutapa and Torwa represent migrate/transform rather than collapse.
quantitative_anchors: Site occupied c.1100-1450; environmental carrying capacity estimated at ~18,000 maximum (Pikirayi)

MOD data quality reflects reliance on archaeology (no indigenous writing); Indian Ocean trade imports provide dating anchors. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Aksum

P1.justification: King (negus) with provincial administration; one of earliest African states to mint its own coinage (indicating fiscal sophistication). Christianity as state religion from c.340 provided institutional framework. But limited bureaucratic depth compared to Roman/Sasanian contemporaries.
quantitative_anchors: Aksumite coinage: gold, silver, and bronze denominations from c.270-630 CE; Ge'ez script inscriptions document royal governance

P2.justification: Monumental obelisk construction (tallest ~33m), coinage production, Ge'ez script development, and terrace agriculture. Knowledge production comparable to regional peers.
quantitative_anchors: Stelae field: largest obelisk ~33m, ~520 tons (largest monolith attempted in ancient world); coinage produced for ~360 years

P3.justification: Ge'ez literacy in court and church; Christian education infrastructure after conversion. Population estimates uncertain but urban center suggests moderate development.
quantitative_anchors: Aksum city: estimated 20,000-40,000 at peak; Adulis port population perhaps 10,000-20,000

P4.justification: Controlled Red Sea trade between Roman/Byzantine Mediterranean and Indian Ocean; Adulis was major entrepôt. Loss of Red Sea access to Islamic expansion after 7th century is the key P4 collapse.
quantitative_anchors: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st c.) describes Adulis as major port; Aksumite coins found in South Arabia, India; trade in ivory, gold, frankincense

P5.justification: Maintained Red Sea hegemony for ~600 years (1st-7th c. CE). Islamic expansion cut maritime trade routes; polity contracted southward into Ethiopian highlands — a migrate/transform outcome.
quantitative_anchors: Coinage ceases c.630 CE, indicating loss of trade revenue; Aksumite state contracted to Lasta/Zagwe highland successor by 10th century

bibliography: Munro-Hay, S. (1991). Aksum: An African Civilisation of Late Antiquity. Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press.
Phillipson, D.W. (2012). Foundations of an African Civilisation: Aksum and the Northern Horn, 1000 BC - AD 1300. Woodbridge: James Currey.
note: ORDINAL (1-5, relative to contemporaries). Grounded in Phillipson's archaeological synthesis and Munro-Hay's comprehensive study. Coinage evidence provides unusually firm dating and economic anchor for African ancient case. 'Migrate' outcome parallels Angkor. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Aztec Triple Alliance

P1.justification: Triple Alliance was a confederacy (Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, Tlacopan) with tributary extraction but minimal direct administrative penetration of conquered provinces. Hegemonic rather than territorial empire — the archetype of suppression-without-integration.
quantitative_anchors: Codex Mendoza: ~371 tributary provinces; tribute lists quantify extraction but not governance; calpulli (ward) system in core only

P2.justification: Chinampas (floating garden) agriculture, advanced calendrical/astronomical systems, pharmacopoeia, and monumental architecture. Significant knowledge but limited in comparison to Old World contemporaries with printing and metallurgy.
quantitative_anchors: Chinampa agriculture yielded ~3,000 kg/hectare/year (Smith); Templo Mayor: 60m pyramid rebuilt 7 times

P3.justification: Calmecac (elite) and telpochcalli (commoner) schools provided unusually broad education for a pre-modern state; life expectancy ~30-35 years typical of pre-Columbian Mesoamerica.
quantitative_anchors: Tenochtitlan population: 200,000-300,000 (Smith); Valley of Mexico ~1-1.5M; universal male education documented in codices

P4.justification: Extensive tribute economy and long-distance trade networks (pochteca merchants); large market at Tlatelolco served 40,000-60,000 daily. But no coinage — cacao beans and cotton mantles as media of exchange.
quantitative_anchors: Tlatelolco market: Cortés estimated 60,000 daily; Codex Mendoza documents tribute in quantified units; pochteca trade routes extended to Maya lowlands

P5.justification: Alliance endured ~93 years (1428-1521) with endemic tributary rebellion. Spanish conquest exploited structural fragility — Tlaxcalans and other suppressed tributaries allied with Cortés immediately.
quantitative_anchors: 1519-21: Cortés + ~200,000 indigenous allies vs Aztec; structural suppression meant rapid defection of tributaries; smallpox reduced Tenochtitlan by ~40% during siege

bibliography: Berdan, F.F. et al. (1996). Aztec Imperial Strategies. Washington: Dumbarton Oaks.

Peak = pre_stress because collapse was exogenous (Spanish conquest); the P4>P1 gap and confederacy structure made rapid defection predictable. RICH data quality via codices and ethnohistorical sources. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Classic Maya

P1.justification: Network of competing divine-kingship city-states (ajaw system), not a unified empire. Individual polities (Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque) had sophisticated local governance with scribe bureaucracies and diplomatic systems, but no overarching institutional framework.
quantitative_anchors: ~60 emblem glyphs indicating independent polities; Maya script: ~800 distinct glyphs; extensive diplomatic correspondence in hieroglyphic texts

P2.justification: Independent invention of zero, sophisticated long-count calendar, hieroglyphic writing, advanced astronomy, corbel-arch architecture, and intensive raised-field agriculture.
quantitative_anchors: Dresden Codex: Venus tables accurate to 2 hours over 481 years; temple pyramids at Tikal reach 47m

P3.justification: Elite literacy in hieroglyphic script; general population primarily agricultural with access to sophisticated medical/herbal traditions. LiDAR has dramatically revised population estimates upward.
quantitative_anchors: Canuto et al. LiDAR (2018): Maya Lowland population revised upward to 7-11M at Late Classic peak; Tikal urban zone ~60,000-120,000

P4.justification: Long-distance trade in jade, obsidian, cacao, salt, and Spondylus shell; market systems documented but scale limited compared to contemporaneous Old World empires.
quantitative_anchors: Obsidian trade: El Chayal and Ixtepeque sources distributed across 500+ km; cacao as prestige currency

P5.justification: Chronic inter-polity warfare with no stabilizing hegemony; system inherently fragile. Terminal Classic collapse (c.800-1000 CE) correlated with severe drought, soil degradation, and intensified warfare.
quantitative_anchors: Kennett et al. (Science 2012): stalagmite isotope data shows severe droughts c.820-870 CE coinciding with political collapse; ~40 royal courts ceased monument construction within ~100 years

P5 is lowest in the corpus — reflects structurally unstable peer-polity system. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Tiwanaku

P1.justification: State-level polity with monumental ceremonial center (Akapana, Kalasasaya) and administrative colonies in coastal/valley regions. Governance appears ritual-ceremonial rather than bureaucratic — authority through pilgrimage and prestige rather than coercive administration.
quantitative_anchors: Akapana pyramid: 200m x 200m base, 17m height; administrative colonies at Omo (Moquegua), Chen Chen, and Cochabamba Valley

P2.justification: Raised-field (suka qollu) agriculture at 3,800m altitude was a significant innovation; monumental stone architecture and metallurgy present. But no writing system and limited evidence of systematic knowledge accumulation.
quantitative_anchors: Kolata: raised fields covered ~130 km2 around Lake Titicaca; produced 2-3x yields of non-raised plots at altitude

P3.justification: No writing system; population estimates modest. High-altitude adaptation (coca, freeze-dried potato/chuño) demonstrates indigenous knowledge but formal education infrastructure absent.
quantitative_anchors: Tiwanaku urban core: estimated 20,000-40,000; total polity population ~365,000 (Kolata estimate, debated)

P4.justification: Multi-ecological trade network ('vertical archipelago' principle): highland pastoral/agricultural products exchanged with coastal/valley goods. Llama caravans and colonial outposts facilitated exchange.
quantitative_anchors: Omo/Moquegua colonies: 300+ km from capital; marine products, maize, and obsidian traded across ecological zones

P5.justification: Polity endured ~500 years. Janusek argues collapse was primarily political (ritual legitimacy failure and social fragmentation), NOT environmental — contra earlier drought hypothesis. Tagged NOT_environmental to flag this scholarly debate.
quantitative_anchors: Ortloff & Kolata (1993) proposed drought c.1000 CE; Janusek (2008) argues raised-field abandonment preceded drought, indicating political causes

bibliography: Browman, D. (1997). 'Political Institutional Factors Contributing to the Integration of the Tiwanaku State.' World Archaeology 29(1): 117-128.

note: ORDINAL (1-5, relative to contemporaries). Grounded in Kolata's raised-field data and Janusek's political-collapse thesis. NOT_environmental tag flags active scholarly debate (Ortloff & Kolata drought vs Janusek political). MOD data quality; no writing system. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Wari

P1.justification: The unusual P1 inversion (pre_stress > peak) reflects Schreiber's thesis: Wari over-centralized by absorbing provincial autonomy, which paradoxically weakened resilience. Peak P1=2 because the centralized apparatus lacked adaptive capacity once the center weakened.
quantitative_anchors: Huari capital: ~15 km2 urban area; D-shaped administrative buildings replicated at provincial centers (Pikillacta, Viracochapampa)

P2.justification: Road and administrative architecture; textile production and metallurgy present. But less evidence of systematic knowledge production than contemporaneous Tiwanaku; no writing system.
quantitative_anchors: Pikillacta: planned administrative center covering ~2 km2 with 504 buildings; standardized ceramic and textile styles indicate centralized production

P3.justification: No writing system; population estimates modest. High-altitude Andean population with limited evidence of formal education or health infrastructure beyond subsistence.
quantitative_anchors: Total polity population uncertain; Huari urban core perhaps 10,000-40,000 (estimates vary widely)

P4.justification: Multi-craft economy with centralized production and redistribution; road network connected ecological zones. Less commercially oriented than contemporary Tiwanaku.
quantitative_anchors: Nash documents centralized multi-craft production at Cerro Baul; obsidian and Spondylus shell traded across ecological zones

P5.justification: Polity endured ~400 years but collapse was sudden — administrative centers were deliberately burned/abandoned. The centralization_trigger tag reflects how over-centralization created brittleness.
quantitative_anchors: Pikillacta: evidence of deliberate burning and abandonment c.1000 CE; Huari similarly abandoned; no successor state emerged from core

bibliography: Isbell, W.H. & McEwan, G. (1991). 'A History of Huari Studies and Introduction to Current Interpretations.' In W.H. Isbell & G. McEwan (eds), Huari Administrative Structure. Washington: Dumbarton Oaks.

The P1 inversion (pre_stress 3 > peak 2) is deliberate: centralization_trigger thesis — over-centralization reduced adaptive capacity. MOD data quality; no writing system. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Carolingian

P1.justification: Charlemagne's personal authority over counts and missi dominici (royal inspectors) did not survive him as institutional infrastructure. Frankish partible inheritance (frag_engineered) structurally mandated fragmentation. The thinnest institutional container in the European corpus.
quantitative_anchors: ~300 counties (comitatus); missi dominici system documented in capitularies; Ordinatio Imperii (817) attempted but failed to prevent partition

P2.justification: Carolingian Renaissance: monastic scriptoria, Alcuin's educational reforms, and manuscript copying preserved classical learning. But innovation was preservation-focused, not generative.
quantitative_anchors: ~90% of surviving classical Latin texts come from Carolingian copies; Caroline minuscule standardized European handwriting

P3.justification: Literacy confined to clergy; monastic schools the only educational infrastructure. Population recovering from post-Roman demographic collapse; life expectancy ~30 years.
quantitative_anchors: Maddison: Western Europe GDP/cap ~$427 GK$ c.800; population ~25-30M in Carolingian territory (McEvedy & Jones)

P4.justification: Limited monetization (denier silver standard); economy predominantly agrarian and manorial. McCormick documents beginning of Mediterranean/North Sea trade revival but scale was modest.
quantitative_anchors: McCormick: trade revival documented through ~669 datable traveler records 700-900 CE; Dorestad emporium peak ~200 ships/year

P5.justification: United empire lasted only under Charlemagne (r.768-814); Treaty of Verdun (843) partitioned realm into three kingdoms per Frankish inheritance custom. Stability was ruler-dependent, not institutional.
quantitative_anchors: Treaty of Verdun (843): tripartite division into West Francia, Middle Francia, East Francia; Viking raids intensified from 830s

bibliography: Costambeys, M. et al. (2011). The Carolingian World. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
McCormick, M. (2001). Origins of the European Economy: Communications and Commerce AD 300-900. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Lowest overall scores in European subset — 'thin_container' tag is the key diagnostic. Fragmentation was structurally engineered by partible inheritance, not a failure. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Byzantine (Macedonian)

P1.justification: Roman legal inheritance (Basilika legal code, c.892); thematic military-administrative system; professional bureaucracy with logothetes (ministers), eparch (urban prefect), and tax apparatus. Most institutionally continuous pre-modern European state.
quantitative_anchors: Basilika: 60-volume legal code; Book of the Eparch regulated Constantinople's guilds; thematic system divided empire into ~30 military-administrative provinces

P2.justification: Greek fire (state military secret), silk production monopoly, advanced architecture (Hagia Sophia maintenance), and manuscript preservation. More conservation/adaptation than breakthrough innovation.
quantitative_anchors: Greek fire: state secret maintained for centuries; silk monopoly: imperial gynaikeion workshops; Constantinople's university refounded c.863

P3.justification: Highest urban literacy in medieval Europe; Constantinople's educational institutions, church schools, and widespread Greek literacy. Laiou & Morrisson document recovery of living standards during Macedonian dynasty.
quantitative_anchors: Laiou & Morrisson: Byzantine GDP/cap recovered to ~$600-700 GK$ by 10th c. (above W. European levels); Constantinople population ~500,000-800,000

P4.justification: Constantinople as Eurasian trade hub; gold solidus/nomisma the 'dollar of the Middle Ages'; silk trade monopoly; regulated guild economy with sophisticated commercial law.
quantitative_anchors: Laiou & Morrisson: nomisma maintained ~4.5g gold standard for 700 years; Book of the Eparch regulates 22 guild categories

P5.justification: Macedonian dynasty (867-1056) represents 189 years of relative stability and territorial recovery. Thematic system provided resilient military-fiscal base; Basil II's conquests (976-1025) represent peak.
quantitative_anchors: Basil II: conquered Bulgaria (1018), expanded to largest post-Justinianic borders; left treasury surplus of ~200,000 lbs gold

bibliography: Gregory, T. (2010). A History of Byzantium. 2nd ed. Malden: Wiley-Blackwell.
Haldon, J. (2016). The Empire That Would Not Die: The Paradox of Eastern Roman Survival, 640-740. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.

Flat peak/pre_stress profile reflects the 'absorb' outcome — Macedonian dynasty sustained institutional quality without deterioration. Laiou & Morrisson GDP estimates are unusually firm for a medieval case. Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Venetian Republic

P1.justification: Elaborate republican constitution: Great Council, Senate, Council of Ten, Doge (elected, constrained). Puga & Trefler show how colleganza contracts created institutional innovation in commercial law. Highest-P1 ancient case — institutions so strong they outlasted trade dominance.
quantitative_anchors: Great Council: ~2,500 members by 14th c.; Doge elected by 41-member committee through 10-round process; republic endured 1,100 years (697-1797)

P2.justification: Arsenal (state shipyard) pioneered assembly-line production; Murano glass monopoly; printing industry (Aldus Manutius). Peak P2=4 reflects 15th-16th c. innovation zenith; pre_stress P2=3 reflects earlier commercial-focus era.
quantitative_anchors: Arsenal: produced 1 galley/day at peak; employed ~16,000 workers (largest industrial complex in pre-modern Europe); Aldine Press: ~130 first editions

P3.justification: High literacy for pre-modern Europe; extensive notarial/legal documentation culture; University of Padua (under Venetian control) among Europe's leading institutions.
quantitative_anchors: Malanima: northern Italian GDP/cap ~$1,100-1,400 GK$ at peak (14th-15th c.); Venice population ~180,000 at 1340 peak; male literacy estimated 30-40%

P4.justification: Mediterranean trade hegemon: spice/silk monopoly, state-organized merchant convoys (muda), and sophisticated financial instruments. Peak P4=5 reflects 13th-15th c. commercial dominance; pre_stress P4=3 reflects earlier, pre-Crusades era.
quantitative_anchors: Puga & Trefler: colleganza contracts show institutional basis for long-distance trade; annual pepper imports ~1,200 tons at peak; state debt (Monte Vecchio) from 1262

P5.justification: 1,100 years of continuous republican government (697-1797) — longest-lived republic in history. Only ended by Napoleonic conquest (exogenous), not internal fragmentation.
quantitative_anchors: 697-1797: 1,100 years; survived Ottoman threat, League of Cambrai (1508), and plague (1348, 1575, 1630); constitutional stability unique in pre-modern record

note: ORDINAL (1-5, relative to contemporaries). Grounded in Lane's standard history, Puga & Trefler's QJE institutional analysis, and Malanima's GDP estimates. Highest-scoring case in the ancient corpus alongside Song China; P1=5 + P5=5 is the 'durability' archetype. Convergence_closure tag flags Puga & Trefler's finding that institutional openness eventually narrowed (Serrata of 1297). Directional only; firewall from 213C/0F baseline.

name: Ottoman (classical)

P1.justification: Timar land-grant system, devshirme recruitment creating slave-meritocratic elite, provincial eyalet/sanjak administration, codified kanun (secular law) alongside sharia. Sophisticated but not quite reaching Song/Venice institutional depth.
quantitative_anchors: İnalcık: ~37 eyalets by 1600; devshirme recruited ~1,000-3,000 boys per levy; kanunname legal compilations for each province

P2.justification: Rapid adoption of gunpowder weapons, advanced military architecture (star forts), sophisticated cartography (Piri Reis), and institutional innovation in military organization. More adaptive-innovative than purely conservationist.
quantitative_anchors: Topkapi cannon: 8m bronze bombard at Constantinople siege (1453); Piri Reis map (1513) synthesizes 20 source maps; Istanbul population ~400,000-700,000 by 1550

P3.justification: Medrese (theological college) system provided education for ulema class; general population literacy limited. Millet system allowed religious-community self-governance but constrained cross-community human development.
quantitative_anchors: İnalcık: population ~22M by c.1520; Pamuk: Istanbul real wages comparable to European cities; ~150 medrese in Istanbul alone by 1580

P4.justification: Controlled east-west trade routes; monetized economy with akçe silver standard; İnalcık's timar system integrated fiscal-military-agricultural production. Pamuk documents prices and wages comparable to or exceeding European levels.
quantitative_anchors: Pamuk (JEH 2012): Ottoman GDP/cap ~$600-700 GK$ at peak; Istanbul consumer prices systematically recorded; customs revenue from Bursa silk market ~300,000 akçe/year

P5.justification: Classical period (1299-1566) includes 267 years of expansion and consolidation. Devshirme succession mechanism (no primogeniture — most capable son wins fratricidal contest) was brutal but effective at preventing weak rulers.
quantitative_anchors: 10 sultans in 267 years of classical period; survived Timur's defeat (1402) and 11-year Interregnum; Suleiman's death (1566) conventionally marks end of classical era

name: New Kingdom Egypt

P1.justification: At peak (18th-19th Dynasties): professional military, vizier-led bureaucracy, international diplomacy (Amarna Letters). Pre-stress (late 20th Dynasty): priestly autonomy in Thebes, worker strikes, and tomb robberies indicate institutional decay.
quantitative_anchors: Amarna Letters: ~380 clay tablets documenting international diplomacy; Deir el-Medina worker records provide detailed administrative data; Turin Papyrus catalogs state officials

P2.justification: Advanced medicine (Ebers Papyrus), monumental architecture (Valley of the Kings, Abu Simbel), glass-making, and bronze metallurgy. Continuation and refinement of OK/MK knowledge rather than revolutionary innovation.
quantitative_anchors: Abu Simbel: 4 statues at 20m height; Valley of the Kings: 63 royal tombs; Ebers Papyrus: 110 pages of medical knowledge

P3.justification: Scribal literacy perhaps 1-3% of population; Deir el-Medina records show skilled worker community with medical care, education, and regulated labor conditions — but this was an elite community, not representative.
quantitative_anchors: Butzer: population 3-4.5M; Deir el-Medina: ~120 workers with detailed payment records; first documented labor strike (~1157 BCE) under Ramesses III

P4.justification: International trade networks spanning Mediterranean, Nubia, and Punt; tribute economy from conquered territories (Syria, Kush). Bronze Age collapse disrupted these networks catastrophically.
quantitative_anchors: Cline: Late Bronze Age trade network linked Egypt, Hatti, Mycenae, Ugarit, Cyprus; Amarna Letters document international gift exchange; Punt expeditions brought incense, gold, myrrh

P5.justification: Stable for ~300 years (18th-19th Dynasties); Bronze Age collapse (c.1177 BCE) brought Sea Peoples invasions, trade network collapse, and systemic drought. Third Intermediate Period fragmentation followed.
quantitative_anchors: Cline: Sea Peoples attacks c.1177 BCE; Medinet Habu reliefs document battles; Harris Papyrus records Ramesses III's temple donations totaling ~1/3 of cultivable land — institutional capture

bibliography: Butzer, K. (1976). Early Hydraulic Civilization in Egypt. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
Cline, E. (2014). 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed. Princeton: Princeton University Press.

Deir el-Medina records provide unusually rich administrative data for an ancient case. Environmental_systemic tag reflects multi-cause collapse (Sea Peoples + drought + institutional capture).
